content: Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) in neonates is a condition associated with significant rates of mortality and long-term morbidity. Currently, effective treatment options for this condition are limited, which has led to the exploration of alternative therapies, such as acupuncture, as potential interventions. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of acupuncture in reducing mortality and morbidity in neonates diagnosed with HIE. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Cochrane Neonatal Specialized Register, MEDLINE, AMED, EMBASE, PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and various Chinese medical databases. This search was completed in November 2012. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared needle acupuncture to a control group receiving no treatment, placebo, or sham treatment in neonates under 28 days of age with HIE. Trials were permitted to include co-interventions, provided that both the intervention and control groups received the same co-interventions. Studies that evaluated therapies not involving skin penetration with needles or those comparing different forms of acupuncture were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of trials for inclusion. If eligible trials had been identified, the reviewers planned to evaluate the quality of the studies and extract data independently. The analysis would have included calculating risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and the number needed to treat for benefit (NNTB) or harm (NNTH) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for dichotomous outcomes, as well as mean differences (MD) with 95% CI for continuous outcomes. However, no trials met the predefined inclusion criteria. The existing studies on acupuncture were limited to older infants who had survived HIE, and no randomized controlled trials specifically evaluated the efficacy of acupuncture in neonates with HIE. Furthermore, the safety profile of acupuncture in this population remains unknown. The authors concluded that there is no clear rationale for the use of acupuncture in neonates with HIE, as evidence from randomized controlled trials is lacking. Consequently, acupuncture cannot be recommended as a treatment for HIE in neonates at this time. High-quality randomized controlled trials are urgently needed to assess the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for this condition in neonates.
